title: A modular quantum computer based on Cornucopia codes
authors: Zhide Lu, Weikang Li, Yinghao Ma, Hanyu Yan, Bingrun Wang, Yixuan Ma, Zheng-Zhi Sun, Dong-Ling Deng
abstract: Ultra-high-rate quantum error correction codes can store many logical qubits in a single code block with few physical qubits. A fault-tolerant quantum computer, however, also requires a universal set of logical operations on individually addressable logical qubits, and the ancilla overhead of these operations may erode the advantage of the high encoding rate. Here, we propose the Cornucopia architecture, in which a universal set of logical operations is implemented at low overhead for the Cornucopia codes. In particular, we focus on the [[2844,1426,18]] Cornucopia code as an example and introduce a modular quantum computer built from such code blocks connected by bridges. Each block stores 1,426 logical qubits and serves as a universal logical processor. Exploiting the code's translation symmetry, we construct a family of reusable gadgets that individually address 1,422 logical qubits within each block. These gadgets support three universal logical instruction sets: basic, high-throughput and fixed-extractor. Excluding magic-state factories, a module with sufficient workspace to execute any instruction in the basic set requires an average of 4.1 physical qubits per logical qubit, compared with 3.0 for memory alone. The architecture thus preserves the resource advantage of ultra-high-rate quantum memory while enabling universal logical computation, providing a route towards low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computers.
summary: This paper proposes the Cornucopia architecture, a modular design for fault-tolerant quantum computing that merges the high storage density of ultra-high-rate quantum error correcting codes with the capability for universal logical operations. By introducing specialized, reusable gadgets and connection bridges, the authors demonstrate a pathway to achieving low-overhead, scalable quantum computation. This work is significant for advancing the practical realization of large-scale quantum processors.
main_problem: The challenge is designing a fault-tolerant quantum computer architecture that maintains the high resource efficiency of ultra-high-rate quantum error correction codes while supporting universal, low-overhead logical operations.
main_result: The proposed Cornucopia architecture successfully integrates high-rate memory with universal logical computation by implementing three instruction sets (basic, high-throughput, fixed-extractor) with manageable overhead.
method: The authors utilize a modular design based on the Cornucopia code, employing 'code surgery' and symmetry-adapted gadgets to perform logical operations while preserving the code distance.
model_or_system: The system is a modular quantum computer built from interconnected code blocks based on the [[2844,1426,18]] Cornucopia code. Each block acts as a universal logical processor, connected by specialized bridges.
key_observables: Logical error rate ($2.6 	imes 10^{-16}$ per logical qubit per cycle), physical qubits per logical qubit (4.1 for basic set vs. 3.0 for memory alone), and code distance ($d=18$).
important_parameters: Encoding rate (ultra-high, > 1/2), number of logical qubits per block (1,426), and the size of the connecting bridges (18 qubits).
main_assumptions: The construction relies on the ability to build gadgets that provably preserve the code distance and the assumption that the overhead of the basic instruction set is acceptable compared to the memory advantage.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the modular structure, the three instruction sets (basic, high-throughput, fixed-extractor), and the detailed mechanisms for performing logical operations like CNOT gates across module bridges.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first introducing the Cornucopia architecture to solve the overhead problem, detailing the three instruction sets and the use of reusable gadgets, then focusing on inter-module operations (bridges, CNOT), and finally comparing the resource scaling against alternative architectures like the bicycle code.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computation, the rigorous resource accounting and comparison of overheads (e.g., physical qubits per logical qubit) provide quantitative benchmarks relevant to scaling any complex quantum hardware platform.
